Christopher Nolan’s *Oppenheimer* (2023) is an intense, ambitious film that feels especially powerful in IMAX. The huge format makes the Trinity test sequence genuinely overwhelming: the silence before the explosion, the sudden flash of light, and the delayed roar create a physical sense of dread rather than simple spectacle. Ludwig Göransson’s score and the pounding sound design add to the experience without making it feel like a conventional action movie.

Cillian Murphy gives a remarkable performance as J. Robert Oppenheimer, portraying him as brilliant, vain, anxious, and increasingly haunted by the consequences of his work. The supporting cast is exceptional too, particularly Robert Downey Jr. as Lewis Strauss, Emily Blunt as Kitty Oppenheimer, and Matt Damon as General Leslie Groves. The film’s shifting timelines and black-and-white sections initially feel complicated, but they gradually build a compelling picture of how scientific achievement became entangled with politics, ego, and fear.

At three hours, *Oppenheimer* is undeniably long. Some courtroom and security-hearing scenes move slowly, and the dense dialogue demands concentration. Still, the runtime feels mostly justified because the film is covering the Manhattan Project, Oppenheimer’s personal life, and the political fallout over several decades. In IMAX, the scale and detail make the length easier to accept, though it is worth taking a break beforehand. This is not a relaxed historical drama; it is an absorbing, exhausting experience that lingers long after the credits.
output:
Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer (2023) is an epic and very intense film. It really comes into its own when viewed in IMAX as the sheer scale of the experience when seeing the Trinity test is overwhelming. The build-up to the explosion, the flash and the delayed sound of the explosion are genuinely intimidating rather than just being a spectacle. The score by Ludwig Göransson and the thunderous sound design compliment the film without it being a standard action film.

The performances are amazing and are led by a wonderful Cillian Murphy as J. Robert Oppenheimer. He shows Oppenheimer to be a genius, vain, neurotic and increasingly tortured by what he has done. The supporting cast is fantastic. Robert Downey Jr. is great as Lewis Strauss. Emily Blunt as Kitty Oppenheimer and Matt Damon as General Leslie Groves are also very good. While at first it seems confusing and complicated with multiple timelines and black and white segments it gradually coheres and paints a fascinating picture of the interplay of science with politics, ego and fear.

This is a very long film. At 3 hours it's a long sit. There are a few scenes in the court and security hearings which can drag a bit and require you to pay close attention to what can be dense dialog. Ultimately though, the length makes sense as it's not just telling the story of the Manhattan Project. It's telling that story, the personal story of Oppenheimer and the political aftermath of it all over a period of decades. In IMAX the detail and scale helps make it easier to swallow. But perhaps have a break first as it's not a lazy history lesson. It's a fascinating and tiring film. You won't forget it easily.

When the European Recovery Program—better known as the Marshall Plan—was signed into law by President Truman on April 3, 1948, West Germany's economic future looked bleak. Its industrial cities lay in ruins, its currency was nearly worthless, and its economy remained constrained by Allied occupation policies that had capped steel production and dismantled industrial plants. Yet over the next four years, roughly $1.4 billion in Marshall Plan aid flowed into what would become the Federal Republic of Germany, helping to catalyze one of the most remarkable economic recoveries of the twentieth century.

The aid itself, distributed through the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), mattered less for its raw quantity than for its timing and function. West Germany received goods—cotton, wheat, coal, machinery—paid for in nearly worthless Reichsmarks, with the proceeds funneled into a special counterpart fund. This fund, worth several billion Deutschmarks, was later reinvested in infrastructure and industry, helping finance projects like electrical grid modernization and the expansion of the Ruhr Valley's steel sector. Perhaps just as important, Marshall Plan money covered Germany's chronic trade deficit in 1949 and 1950, buying the young West German state time while its currency reform of June 1948—which introduced the Deutschmark—took hold.

The Marshall Plan also forced institutional changes that proved decisive. Acceptance of American aid required participation in the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC), pulling West Germany into a framework of European cooperation that would culminate decades later in the European Coal and Steel Community of 1951. Moreover, American pressure helped soften occupation restrictions: limits on steel production were progressively raised from around 5.8 million tons to over 11 million by the early 1950s, and plant dismantling largely ceased. Economist Ludwig Erhard, appointed Economic Director in 1948, combined this new freedom with his policy of the "social market economy," blending free-market competition with a social safety net.

The results were extraordinary. Industrial production in West Germany roughly doubled between 1948 and 1952, and by the mid-1950s the country was producing more than it had before the war—a phenomenon Chancellor Konrad Adenauer's government celebrated as the "economic miracle," or Wirtschaftswunder. Historians rightly caution that the Marshall Plan was only one cause among many, alongside currency reform, Korean War demand, and a skilled labor force. Still, it is fair to say that American aid did not simply rebuild West Germany's economy; it reoriented it—toward Europe, toward trade, and toward the stable democratic capitalism that would define the Federal Republic for generations.
output:
On April 3, 1948, President Truman signed into law the European Recovery Program (Marshall Plan). At the time, the economic outlook for West Germany was grim. Much of the industrial heartland was destroyed. The currency had virtually no value. The economy was still hamstrung by Allied policies that had limited steel output and deindustrialized the country. But in the next four years, the Federal Republic of Germany would receive about $1.4 billion of Marshall Plan assistance to help propel it into one of the greatest economic turnarounds of the 20th century.

The aid, managed by the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) did not come so much in the amount of assistance received, as in the timing and the role of the money. The Federal Republic of Germany was given goods such as cotton, wheat, coal and machinery. The goods were purchased with near-worthless Reichsmarks and the receipts were placed into a special counterpart fund. Later, this fund (several billion Deutschmarks) was reinvested into infrastructure and industry, financing such projects as the modernization of the electrical grid and the development of the Ruhr Valley steel industry. Also, critical to the recovery was that the Marshall Plan funds helped fill West Germany's yawning trade deficit in 1949 and 1950, giving the new state of West Germany time for its June 1948 currency reform (new currency, the Deutschmark) to take effect.

Crucial to the economic recovery was the way that the Marshall Plan created institutional change. For one thing, in order to take U.S. assistance, West Germany had to join the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC). This meant that West Germany was being linked into European cooperation that would ultimately lead, decades later, to the 1951 European Coal and Steel Community. The U.S. also used pressure to relax occupation restrictions. Restrictions on steel output were increased gradually from about 5.8 million to over 11 million tons by the early 1950s. Dismantling of industrial facilities largely stopped. Economic Director (appointed in 1948) Ludwig Erhard took advantage of this and instituted his "social market economy." Free-market competition would be combined with a social safety net.

The results were dramatic. Between 1948 and 1952, industrial output in West Germany rose roughly two-fold. By the mid-1950s, West Germany's output surpassed pre-war levels. This was something that Chancellor Konrad Adenauer's government would tout as the "economic miracle," Wirtschaftswunder. Certainly, historians are careful to note that the Marshall Plan was just one of many factors that contributed to the recovery. Also important were currency reform, increased demand due to the Korean War and a workforce skilled in industrial production. But it is fair to say that not only did U.S. assistance revive West Germany's economy, it transformed it. It turned it towards Europe, it turned it towards trade. And it transformed it towards a stable form of democratic capitalism that would be the hallmark of the Federal Republic for many years to come.

For a freelance designer, I’d aim for 6–12 months of essential personal expenses, not an arbitrary dollar amount. Irregular income makes the upper end more appropriate than the usual three-month target.

For example, if you live in Portland, Oregon, and your bare-bones monthly costs are:

- Rent and utilities: $1,800
- Health insurance and medical costs: $500
- Food: $500
- Transportation: $250
- Minimum debt payments and other necessities: $150

Your essential budget is $3,200 per month. A reasonable emergency-fund target would therefore be $19,200 for six months, with $28,800 providing a stronger 9-month cushion.

Keep separate accounts for three different purposes:

1. Emergency fund: job gaps, illness, or major unexpected expenses.
2. Tax reserve: money for quarterly federal and state estimated taxes.
3. Business reserve: software, equipment replacement, subcontractors, and slow client payments.

Otherwise, a large tax bill or broken laptop can make your “emergency fund” look healthier than it really is.

I’d calculate the target using your lowest realistic monthly spending, not your average lifestyle. Pay yourself a consistent amount—say $4,000 monthly—from your business account, and send unusually strong months into savings. Refill the fund after using it, and keep it in an easily accessible FDIC-insured savings account rather than investments.

The CFPB specifically identifies emergency funds as useful for people with irregular income, while the FDIC cites three to six months as a general guideline and notes that people with especially uncertain employment may need six months or more. [CFPB guidance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/an-essential-guide-to-building-an-emergency-fund/) and [FDIC guidance](https://www.fdic.gov/consumer-resource-center/2025-01/saving-unexpected-and-your-future).
output:
As a freelance designer I think you'd want 6-12 months of core living expenses rather than a dollar number.  The irregular income means you'd want more than the typical 3-month emergency fund amount.
So say, if you're in Portland, Oregon and your absolutely-barebones monthly expenses are:
- Rent & utilities: $1800
- Health insurance & health costs: $500
- Food: $500
- Transportation: $250
- Debt minimums & other necessities: $150

So your core expenses are $3200/month.  So you'd want something like $19.2k for 6 months emergency fund or a stronger $28.8k for 9 months.
Have separate accounts for 3 types of things:
1) Emergency fund: gaps in work, sickness, major unexpected expenses
2) Tax buffer: For quarterly federal & state estimated tax payments
3) Business buffer: Software & equipment replacement. Subcontractors.  Slow clients.
Otherwise you'll have a big tax bill or busted laptop and then your "emergency" fund looks better than it actually is.
Figure out your target based on your minimum real-world monthly expenses.  Not average lifestyle.  Set yourself a regular salary (e.g. $4k/month) to draw from business account and save on those really good months.  Replenish the fund when you draw from it.  Make it a liquid FDIC savings account.  Not investments.
CFPB directly mentions emergency funds as good for irregular income folks.  FDIC mentions 3-6 months as a good guideline in general.  Also mentions if you're really uncertain about employment you may need 6+ months. [cfpb guidance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/an-essential-guide-to-building-an-emergency-fund/) [fdic guidance](https://www.fdic.gov/consumer-resource-center/2025-01/saving-unexpected-and-your-future)

在杭州做了5年全职妈妈后，我重新找工作的72小时

周一早上8点，我把女儿送到滨江的幼儿园，站在门口深吸一口气，打开了尘封5年的招聘软件。

简历改到凌晨一点。老公阿哲说：“你这5年的空白期，HR会问的。”我在“工作经历”里补了一行：“2020-2025 独立运营家庭及社区项目”——听起来体面，其实就是带娃加组织了三年小区团购。

周二上午接到第一个面试电话，是滨江一家电商公司招运营。对方问：“孩子谁带？”我说婆婆每周来帮忙三天。电话那头沉默了两秒：“我们加班比较多。”我说我可以加班，孩子爸爸也在杭州工作。她说“回去等通知”，我就知道没戏了。

周三下午，第二家，武林广场附近的MCN公司。面试官是个94年的姑娘，看完我2019年做的双11活动复盘，眼睛亮了：“数据sense还在啊。”她没问我结没结婚，只问：“薪资预期？”我说了个比5年前低20%的数，她笑了：“我们给到的是你原来的数。”

周四中午offer到了。走出幼儿园接娃的路上，我在钱塘江边哭了十分钟。

5年，我以为自己被职场淘汰了，其实只是被暂停了。妈妈们，别怕，你的能力一直在。

5年杭州全职妈妈，找工作72小时

周一早上8点送完滨江幼儿园女儿，我站在大门外吸了一口气，开启了自己沉寂了5年的招聘软件。

改简历熬到凌晨1点。老公阿哲说：“5年你这空白期HR会问你。”

于是我在“工作经历”这一栏加了一条：2020-2025 独立运营家庭/社区项目

（听起来很高级其实就是带娃组织小区团购3年啦）

周二上午接到了第一个面试电话。

是滨江这边一个电商公司，要招运营。

“我婆婆一个礼拜过来三天”

电话那边停顿了两秒，“我们加班挺多的”

“我能加班，我娃爸也在杭州工作”

“回去等通知”

“……”

知道没戏了

周三下午第二个面试。

MCN公司。

武林广场附近。

面试是个94年的妹子。

她看着我双11的活动复盘2019年做的。

眼睛一亮。

“数据sense还在啊”

她没问我结婚没。

只问我“薪资预期？”

我说我比5年前低20%吧。

她笑了一下：“我们给你的薪资还是你原来的。”

周四中午offer拿到了。

走出来接娃在钱塘江边哭10分钟。

妈妈们别害怕！

你的能力在的。
